"Leave out" has two core meanings in everyday English, plus one bonus informal use. Think of the phrase in two separate directions:

  1. To not include something or someone (the most common meaning by far)
  2. To not put something away — to keep it in an open or visible place
Meaning 1: To Not Include — To Omit or Exclude

This is the heart of the phrasal verb. When you "leave something out," you don't include it. You skip it, remove it, or forget to add it.

When used for things (to omit):

Think of it like building a list, a story, a recipe, or a plan. Everything you don't put in has been left out.

  • "She explained the whole situation but left out the most important detail."
  • "Don't leave out any steps when you follow the instructions."
  • "The editor left out three paragraphs from the article."
  • "Tell me everything — leave nothing out."

A simple mental image: imagine you're packing a bag for a trip. Everything that stays home — everything you didn't pack — has been left out.

When used for people (to exclude):

"Leave out" is equally powerful when talking about people being excluded from a group, a team, an event, or a plan.

  • "The coach left him out of the starting lineup."
  • "Why was she left out of the meeting? Nobody told her about it."
  • "They planned the whole trip and left me out completely."

One of the most frequently used expressions with this verb is "feel left out" or "be left out." It describes the emotional experience of being excluded or ignored — that painful feeling when others don't include you.

  • "All her friends went to the party without inviting her. She felt completely left out."
  • "The new student was quiet because he felt left out."
  • "I always feel left out when they talk about movies I've never seen."

This is real, everyday English. You will hear and read this constantly, so make sure you know it well.
A Special, Very Common Expression: "Leave Me Out of It"

When someone says "leave me out of it," they are saying: don't involve me in this situation. They want no part of something — usually a conflict, a problem, or some drama.

  • "You two can argue all you want — leave me out of it."
  • "This is between you and your boss. Please leave me out of it."

It's a firm but polite way of stepping back from something.
The Grammar: How to Use It Correctly

"Leave out" is a separable phrasal verb. This means the two words — leave and out — can be split apart, with the object placed in the middle.

You have two options:

Option A — Object comes after "out":
"She left out the details."

Option B — Object comes between "leave" and "out":
"She left the details out."

Both are perfectly correct and mean the same thing.

However, there is one firm rule: when the object is a pronoun (it, them, him, her, us, me), you must split the verb. The pronoun cannot go after "out."

✅ Correct → "Leave it out." / "She left him out." / "Don't leave them out."
❌ Wrong → "Leave out it." / "She left out him." / "Don't leave out them."

This rule applies to all separable phrasal verbs in English, not just "leave out."

Using "of" after "leave out":

When you talk about excluding someone or something from a specific group, place, or thing, you follow "out" with the preposition "of":

  • "He was left out of the team."
  • "She left that chapter out of the book."
  • "Don't leave anything out of your report."

Without "of," the sentence feels incomplete when a specific group is mentioned.

Active vs. Passive — Both Are Common:

You'll encounter "leave out" in both the active and passive form:

  • Active: "They left her out of the project."
  • Passive: "She was left out of the project."

Both versions are extremely natural and widely used.
Meaning 2: To Not Put Something Away

This second meaning is quite different and easy to understand once you see it. When you "leave something out," you keep it in an open or accessible place instead of storing it away properly.

  • "Don't leave the milk out — it'll go bad." (Put it back in the fridge.)
  • "She left her clothes out on the chair instead of hanging them up."
  • "I'll leave a key out on the table for you." (I'll keep it there where you can find it.)
  • "Don't leave food out overnight. It will attract insects."

The context almost always makes this meaning clear. The key question to ask yourself is: Is the speaker talking about not including something, or about not putting something away? That question will always point you to the right meaning.

If you ever hear British people say "Leave it out!" as a sharp exclamation, it means something completely different from everything above. It's a casual, informal way of saying:

  • "Stop it!"
  • "Don't be ridiculous!"
  • "Give me a break!"
  • "That's nonsense!"

It's used when someone says something unbelievable, over the top, or annoying.

  • A: "I heard you ate ten burgers in one sitting!"
    B: "Leave it out! It was only three."
  • A: "Just redo the entire website by tomorrow. Shouldn't take long."
    B: "Leave it out — that'll take weeks!"

This is rooted in British (particularly Cockney/London) informal speech. You may not hear it much outside the UK, but you should recognize it when you do.
The Differences Between Meaning 1 and Meaning 2 — Side by Side

These two meanings can occasionally look similar on the surface, so here's how to tell them apart:

"Leave out the salt" → Don't include salt in the recipe. (Meaning 1 — omit)

"Leave the salt out on the counter" → Don't put the salt away; keep it there. (Meaning 2 — not put away)

The position of the object and the surrounding context will almost always make the meaning obvious.

Mistake 1 — Pronoun after "out":
❌ "Leave out it" → ✅ "Leave it out"
❌ "She left out them" → ✅ "She left them out"

Mistake 2 — Forgetting "of" before a group:
❌ "She was left out the team." → ✅ "She was left out of the team."
❌ "He left that detail out the email." → ✅ "He left that detail out of the email."

Here is everything "leave out" can mean, gathered in one place:

To omit something — not include it in a list, story, recipe, plan, etc.
"Don't leave out any steps."

To exclude a person — not include them in a group or activity.
"They left her out of the decision."

To feel left out / be left out — to feel socially excluded.
"He felt left out because no one spoke to him."

"Leave me out of it" — don't involve me in this.
"This is your fight, not mine — leave me out of it."

To not put something away — to keep it in an open place.
"Don't leave the food out — put it in the fridge."

"Leave it out!" (British informal) — Stop it! / Don't be ridiculous!
"Leave it out! That story can't possibly be true."

Master these five uses, follow the grammar rules about pronouns and "of," and you will have complete, confident control over this phrasal verb in any situation.
